INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are religious organizations with a profound
interest in the robust application of the Constitution’s
guarantee of religious freedom. We are particularly
concerned that the misapplication of ripeness doctrine
in this case will inflict lasting damage to the principle
that federal courts stand ready to vindicate First
Amendment rights. Some amici have joined briefs
defending related principles in First Choice Women’s
Resource Centers, Inc. v. Davenport, 146 S. Ct. 1114
(2026); Mahmoud v. Taylor, 606 U.S. 522 (2025); and
Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767 (2022).
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
No American should have to get a permit before
praying with ten fellow believers in his home. Yet
when the City of Universi ty Heights learned that
Daniel Grand had invited f ellow Orthodox Jews to
pray together on the Sabbath, the City Law Director
sent him a cease-and-desist letter. Praying without a
permit, the letter warned, would be a crime. The same
mayor who commissioned the letter hired a private
investigator to monitor Orthodox Jewish residents on
Rosh Hashanah, to determine whether they worshipped
at home with other Jews. See Reply App. 35–37.
But when Grand challenged the City’s actions as a
violation of his freedom to exercise religion and
freedom of assembly, his claims were dismissed as
unripe. That remarkable conclusion misapprehends
ripeness doctrine, which welcomes substantial First
Amendment claims rather than thwarting them.

1 No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and no entity or person, aside from amici, their members,
and their counsel, made any monetary contribution toward the
preparation or submission of this brief.

2
The City’s suppression of Grand’s religious exercise
is hardly the exclusive concern of Orthodox Jewish
communities. Christians, Muslims, and other faiths
also gather with the faithful at home to celebrate, to
worship, and to join in religious ritual together. All
would face the irreparable loss of First Amendment
rights if other local governments choose, like the City,
to single out religious mino rities for unprecedented
administrative burdens and the threat of criminal
prosecution.
The question presented frames the City’s First
Amendment violations under the constitutional chill
doctrine. The record bolsters that claim by attesting to
the City’s violation of the Free Exercise Clause’s
principle of non-persecution. Under that principle, no
government official may target religious belief or
practice for special penalties or burdens. City officials
crossed that line by th reatening Grand with
administrative penalties and criminal prosecution for
practicing his religion.
Yet the Sixth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of
Grand’s complaint as unripe. The court of appeals
accepted the City’s contentions that Williamson
County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton
Bank of Johnson City , 473 U.S. 172 (1985), requires
Grand to produce a “final decision” and that he cannot
meet that test because he withdrew his permit
application after concluding that “the permit would
require him to convert his home into a house of
worship” where he could no longer live. Reply at 2.
But this is a First Amendment case—not a land use
dispute. Grand’s complaint alleges that the City
violated his rights to the fr ee exercise of religion
and to peaceable assembly in his home. Properly
categorized under the First Amendment, this case is

3
unquestionably ripe. Grand can show that he intends
to engage in constitutionally protected activity
allegedly proscribed by law and that he faces a credible
threat of enforcement. The City’s issuance of a ceaseand-desist letter and the mayor’s personal threat of
criminal prosecution amply satisfy that test.
Reviving Grand’s complaint is necessary but
insufficient to protect religious people and institutions.
Williamson County must be strictly limited to claims
under the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause. Allowing
its finality requirement to drift out of its doctrinal lane
condemns First Amendment claims to second-class
status when they bear a superficial nexus to land use.
Grand is not the first litigant with First Amendment
claims to be denied judicial review because of
Williamson County’s misapplication—but let him be
the last. The Sixth Circuit’s judgment should be
reversed and Grand’s complaint heard on the merits.
ARGUMENT
I. G RAND’S FIRST AMENDMENT CLAIMS IMPLICATE
IN-HOME RELIGIOUS PRACTICES CHERISHED
BY DIVERSE FAITHS.
The City’s suppression of Grand’s religious exercise
is hardly the exclusive concern of the Orthodox Jewish
community. Many religions require or encourage the
faithful to study, celebrate, worship, and observe
sacred rituals at home—at times with others.
Declaring Grand’s claims unripe, as the Sixth Circuit
did, risks making a widely  held religious practice
unprotected under the First Amendment.

4
A. Christians Have Worshipped at Home
from the Beginning.
For Christians, the practice of worshiping with
others in private homes traces its roots to Jesus Christ
himself, who promised his disciples that “where two or
three are gathered in my name, there I am among
them.” Matthew 18:20 (English Standard Version).
After Pentecost, Christians were “day by day,
attending the temple together and breaking bread in
their homes”—likely referring to the ritual of the
Lord’s Supper or Eucharist. Acts 2:46 (English
Standard Version). The Apostles preached the Gospel
“every day, in the temple and from house to house .”
Acts 5:42 (English Standard Version) (emphasis
added). And Paul’s letters mention a “church” or
“assembly” in the “house” of prominent Christians
such as Philemon in Colossae, Nympha in Laodicea, or
Prisca and Aquila in Rome. Philemon 1:2; Colossians
4:15; Romans 16:3–5 (English Standard Version).
Scholars generally agree that “[d]uring the first and
second centuries [A.D.] Christians * * * met in homes
and continued to meet primarily in domestic space
until at least such time as the first buildings dedicated
to Christian use begin to appear in the archaeological
record during the course of the third century [A.D.].”
Bradly S. Billings, From House Church to Tenement
Church: Domestic Space and the Development of Early
Urban Christianity , 62 J. Theological Stud. 541, 543
(2011). As late as the third and fourth centuries,
“Christians may not have modified their buildings for
meeting purposes, but simply continued to meet in the
homes of their wealthiest members.” Kim Bowes, Early
Christian Archaeology: A State of the Field , 2 Relig.
Compass 575, 581 (2008).

5
This tradition of worshiping at home persists in
America today. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latterday Saints teaches that “[t]he ideal place to learn the
gospel is the home” and encourages members to study
scripture “with your family, or with friends.” Come,
Follow Me—For Home and Church: Old Testament
2026, at 2 (2026). “[Y]oung singles, single adults, single
parents, part-member fam ilies, [and] new members”
are encouraged “to gather in groups outside the
normal Sunday worship services to enjoy gospel
sociality and be strengthened by studying together.”2
For Southern Baptists, religious exercise has never
been confined to the church sanctuary. Following the
example of the early church, which gathered publicly
and “from house to house,” Acts 5:42, Southern Baptists
routinely open their homes for Bible studies and small
groups, prayer meetings, church planting, youth
gatherings, discipleship groups, missionary gatherings,
hymn singing and worship, and the potluck meals and
fellowship that have long b een a hallmark of Baptist
community. See On the Legacy and Responsibility of
Women Fulfilling the Great Commission , S. Baptist
Convention Res. 5, at 73–75 (June 14, 2023).
Certain large Protestant congregations also encourage
believers to meet as small groups in private homes for
prayer and Bible study. See, e.g., Kevin D. Dougherty
& Andrew L. Whitehead, A Place to Belong: Small
Group Involvement in Religious Congregations, 72 Socio.
Relig. 91, 93, 99 (2011) (small groups are “a prevalent

2 Quentin L. Cook, Deep and Lasting Conversion to Heavenly
Father and the Lord Jesus Christ , Liahona (Nov. 2018),
https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/liahona/2018/11/satur
day-morning-session/deep-and-lasting-conversion-to-heavenlyfather-and-the-lord-jesus-christ?lang=eng.

6
feature of the Protestant megachurch movement”;
some small groups meet in members’ homes).
Millions of Americans participate in the “housechurch movement.” These Christians eschew dedicated
worship spaces and formal church organizations,
believing that informal home gatherings reflect the
New Testament’s ecclesiology. See Roger W. Gehring,
House Church and Mission 295 (2004) (explaining how
in early Christian history, “the house served as the
basic foundation for all church life”). According to the
movement’s advocates, “House churches make room
for the spiritual gifts of all believers to operate on a
regular basis. * * * By gathering simply and naturally
in home-sized groups, everyone becomes a participant
and every person’s gift is  needed.” Roger Thoman,
Simple / House Church Revolution  6–7 (rev. version
1.1 2008).
And most Amish groups do not build church
buildings. Instead, Amish families take turns hosting
services for their church districts, typically in “private
homes, shops, and barns.” Scot E. Long & Richard
Moore, Amish Church District Fissioning and Watershed
Boundaries Among Holmes County, Ohio, Amish , 2 J.
Amish & Plain Anabaptist Stud. 186, 187 (2014).
B. Home Worship Is Important to Non-
Christians Too.
Nor is home-centered worship limited to Christians.
Ninety-seven percent of American Muslims say they
have a mosque nearby, but only 27% say their mosque
is central to their spiritual life. Pew Rsch. Ctr., U.S.
Muslims Concerned About Their Place in Society, but
Continue to Believe in the American Dream  109–10
(2017). Some of the most im portant Muslim religious
practices take place in the home—in particular, most

7
of their five daily prayers ( salat). Trevan G. Hatch et
al., Muslim Families in the United States , in L.D.
Marks & D.C. Dollahite, Religion and Families: An
Introduction 157, 165–67 (2017).
American Muslims’ annual celebration of Ramadan
is also centered on the home. One follower of Islam
reports what appears to be a common experience for
members of his faith community. “[W]e get up early,
very early in the morning to have a meal together, like
a breakfast. We have a meal together, and then after
the meal, we read Qu’ran, our scripture. And after we
do that, it’s time for prayer.” Id. at 169. Ramadan also
includes “a festive evening meal, called ift ār, after
sundown.”3 For that meal, “Muslims gather in their
homes or mosques to break their fast, often joyfully
shared with friends and extended family.”4 One scholar
describes her own growing-up experience, with “the
food, copious amounts of food cooked during Ramadan,
iftars for so many friends and relatives.” Mona
Siddiqui, Hospitality and Islam: Welcoming in God’s
Name 98 (2015).
Hindus likewise worship at home. Seventy-nine
percent of American Hindus “say they use an altar,
shrine, or religious symbol for worship in their home.”
Pew Rsch. Ctr., Religion Among Asian Americans  38
(2023). “For a Hindu, home, besides being a place to
live, is a repository of devotional icons, objects, and
artifacts for which the family altar is the most notable
location. * * * It is in front of the home altar that a
Hindu sits cross-legged on the bare/carpeted floor or
on a prayer mat and seeks communion with his/her

3 Ramadan, Encyclopedia Britannica,  https://www.britannica.
com/topic/Ramadan (last visited Aug. 26, 2026).
4 Ibid.

8
deity, engages in prayer, or in quiet meditation.”
Shampa Mazumdar & Sanjoy Mazumdar, Religion,
Immigration, and Home Making in Diaspora: Hindu
Space in Southern California , 29 J. Env’t Psych. 256,
259 (2009). Such home-based worship often involves
non-family members. “When Indian Hindus [in the
U.S.] celebrate major religious holidays or perform
important family life-cycle rituals at home, they
usually invite relatives and friends, which is one of the
ways that Indian Hindu immigrants maintain kin and
friendship networks.” Pyong Gap Min, Preserving
Ethnicity Through Religion in America: Korean
Protestants and Indian Hindus Across Generations
119 (2010).
Some religious minorities must worship at home
because a religious building is unavailable. When
there is no Baha’i center nearby, Baha’is are encouraged to “hold regular devotional meetings * * *
elsewhere, including the homes of believers.” 5 In a
country with fewer than 180,000 Baha’is, the absence
of a local Baha’i center will often prompt home
worship. Clifford Grammich et al., 2020 U.S. Religion
Census: Religious Congregations & Adherents Study
88 (2023). Similarly, when a Sikh community lacks
enough followers to build a gurdwara—the equivalent
of a chapel or synagogue—b elievers may gather to
worship in a gurdwara set up in a local family’s home.6

5 Universal House of Justice, Selected Guidance Concerning
Devotional Gatherings , ¶ 3, Baha’i Libr. Online, https://bahailibrary.com/uhj_devotional_meetings_compilation (last visited
Aug. 26, 2026).
6 The Pluralism Project at Harvard Univ., The Gurdwara  1
(2020),

9
C. The City’s Targeting of Grand for
Worshiping at Home Threatens Many
Religious Americans.
Exercising religion at home with fellow believers is
thus a religious practice shared by Orthodox Jews,
Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs, and Baha’is. All
pray, worship, celebrate, and gather with fellow
believers in homes. The injuries Grand has suffered for
attempting to pray without a permit could be imposed
on many other religious Americans. They too could
face the irreparable loss of First Amendment rights if
another local government chooses, like the City, to
single out an unpopular religion for unprecedented
administrative burdens and the threat of criminal
prosecution.
That prospect defies the Constitution.
The very purpose of a Bill of Rights was to
withdraw certain subjects from the vicissitudes of political controversy, to place them
beyond the reach of majorities and officials
and to establish them as legal principles to be
applied by the courts. One’s right to life,
liberty, and property, to free speech, a free
press, freedom of worship and assembly, and
other fundamental rights may not be
submitted to vote; they depend on the outcome
of no elections.
W. Va. State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624, 638
(1943) (emphasis added).
Grand’s central claims—that the City chilled his
rights to the free exercise of religion and freedom of

https://pluralism.org/sites/g/files/omnuum10836/files/pluralism/fi
les/the_gurdwara.pdf.

10
assembly—should have received prompt judicial
review. That his claims were dismissed as unripe is
inconsistent with the City’s pronounced animus
against him because of his faith.
II. TARGETING HOME-CENTERED RELIGIOUS
EXERCISE VIOLATES THE FIRST AMENDMENT’S
“NON-PERSECUTION” PRINCIPLE.
A. The First Amendment Prohibits the
Government from Targeting Religious
Beliefs and Practices as Such.
The record shows that the City targeted Grand for
distinctive burdens and penalties because of his
religion—a violation of the Free Exercise Clause that
also “objectively chill[ed]” his First Amendment rights.
First Choice , 146 S. Ct. at 1127. The demand that
Grand apply for a Special Use Permit before
conducting a prayer service in his home unquestionably singled him out. “If Grand’s next-door neighbor
invited nine friends over for a weekly poker night or a
Tupperware party, the City would not require a special
permit to operate a ‘casino’ or ‘storefront.’ The City
targets only Grand’s religious practice.” Reply at 1–2
(citation omitted).
Government targeting of this kind plainly violates
the Free Exercise Clause. “[A] law targeting religious
beliefs as such is never permissible.” Church of the
Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah , 508 U.S.
520, 533 (1993) (emphasis added). “If the object of a
law is to infringe upon or restrict practices because of
their religious motivation,” the First Amendment
imposes a clear bar. Id. “Official action that targets
religious conduct” at home “for distinctive treatment”
falls squarely within this rule. Id. at 534.

11
This anti-targeting principle “is so well understood
that few violations are re corded in [this Court’s]
opinions.” Id. at 523. Encompassed within “this
fundamental nonpersecution principle of the First
Amendment” is a prohibition on laws that “target
religious beliefs” or practices “as such.” Id. at 523, 533.
“Legislators may not devise mechanisms, overt or
disguised, designed to pe rsecute or oppress a religion
or its practices.” Id. at 547.
Lukumi illustrates the rule. There, city ordinances
made animal sacrifice a crime despite its importance
to a small religious minority. But the ordinances
exempted animal slaughter for the purpose of kosher
compliance and for food. Id. at 527–28. Although the
ordinances did not discriminate against religion on
their face, a closer look revealed that the law “singled
out” the religious practices of religious adherents “for
discriminatory treatment.” Id. at 538. “[A]lmost the
only conduct subject to” the ordinances was that
religious exercise. Id. at 535. The city’s purported
rationale for the ordinances could be achieved by other
means that did not impair those religious practices,
and the ordinances were enacted “in direct response to
the opening” of a local church. Id. at 535–40. From
these facts, the Court concluded that the ordinances
were “an impermissible attempt to target” the
religious minority “and [i ts] religious practices” in
violation of the First Amendment. Id. at 535.
Also consider Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado
Civil Rights Commission, 584 U.S. 617 (2018). There, a
state commission sanctioned a baker who declined for
religious reasons to create a custom artistic cake for a
same-sex wedding. Id. at 629–31. This Court held that
the commission violated the First Amendment’s
requirement of religious neutrality in two ways. First,

12
the commission demonstrated “clear and impermissible hostility” toward the baker’s “sincere religious
beliefs” by calling them “despicable” and comparing
them to “defenses of slavery and the Holocaust.” Id. at
635. Second, the commission did not sanction “other
bakers who objected to a requested cake on the basis
of conscience” but for non-religious reasons. Id. at 636.
Glaring “disparity in treatment,” the Court explained,
was further “indication of hostility” by the commission.
Id. at 636–37.
Lukumi and Masterpiece Cakeshop demonstrate the
operation of the non-persecution principle. Government
action that seeks to suppress religious exercise, or that
grows out of religious animus, is void.
B. The City Violated the First Amendment’s Non-Persecution Principle.
That non-persecution principle applies here. A close
review of the record shows how the City, its Planning
Commission, its mayor, and other residents acting at
the mayor’s behest all wo rked to suppress Grand’s
exercise of religion out of animus toward his beliefs
and practices. A few facts stand out.
First, the City’s hostile treatment of Grand’s
attempt to worship at home with fellow believers was
unprecedented. One day after emailing 15 friends to
invite them to pray at his home on the upcoming
Sabbath, Grand received both a cease-and-desist letter
from the City’s attorney and a phone call from the
mayor warning him that the City would take legal
action if he went forward with his plans. Reply App. 9–
11. “[C]ountless residents” had invited groups of
friends to their homes before, but the City had “never
before sent a cease-and-desist letter before the
meeting took place, if at all.” Id. at 12–13. The

13
Planning Commission then conducted the hearing on
Grand’s application in a novel “quasi-judicial” format
that prevented Grand from submitting additional
evidence in support of his application and ensured that
any appeal would be unsuccessful. Pet. App.  29a, 32a;
Reply App. 17–18, 21–22. This treatment reflected
overt hostility toward Grand’s religious exercise. See
Lukumi, 508 U.S. at 540–42; Masterpiece Cakeshop ,
584 U.S. at 636–38.
Second, the City has engaged in discriminatory
treatment of Grand and other Jewish residents. Only
Orthodox Jews are required to have Special Use
Permits to hold gatherings at home. See Reply App. 30
(City official admitting that “[w]e don’t require other
social gatherings occurring in a private home to have
a special use permit”). The mayor even hired a private
investigator to surveil Orthodox Jewish residents on
Rosh Hashanah to determine whether they were
worshipping at home with other Jews. Id.  at 35–37.
That disparate treatment shows that the City has
restricted Jewish practices “because of their religious
nature.” Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 522,
533 (2021).
The City also discriminated at the hearing on
Grand’s application. The Planning Commission entered
into the record a petition opposing Grand’s application
signed by 195 non-Jewish residents but refused to
enter into the record petitions supporting Grand,
including one signed by 240 Jewish residents. Reply
App. 29. The Commission further described the
opposition to Grand as the will of the “community”
while ignoring the hundreds of Jewish residents who
supported Grand. Ibid. This blatant religious
discrimination was, to say the least, a “departure[]

14
from [the] neutrality” that the First Amendment
commands. Masterpiece Cakeshop, 584 U.S. at 638.
Third, the City targeted Grand for seeking to
exercise his religion. It th reatened to invalidate an
already approved variance for Grand’s property if he
held a prayer service at his home. Pet. App.  116a. The
mayor encouraged neighbors to spy on Grand and
report any potential violations to the City. Id. at 143a;
Reply App. 23. The mayor also personally reviewed
surveillance footage of Grand’s home provided by
neighbors and refused to halt the invasion of Grand’s
privacy. Id. at 33–34. The police department directed
officers to “make frequent drive-bys” of Grand’s house.
Id. at 32. And the City Prosecutor coordinated with one
of Grand’s neighbors in an unsuccessful scheme to find
housing violations inside Grand’s home. Id. at 44–46.
The prosecutor promised the neighbor that “[b]etween
the mayor’s office, the housing department, and my
office, we are all pressing forward as urgently as we
can.” Id. at 45–46.
“[E]ven ‘subtle departures from neutrality’ on
matters of religion” are forbidden, Masterpiece Cakeshop,
584 U.S. at 638 (quoting Lukumi, 508 U.S. at 534)—
and there was nothing subtle about the City’s conduct
here. That conduct plainly breached the non-persecution principle and so is “odious to our Constitution, and
cannot stand.” Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia,
Inc. v. Comer, 582 U.S. 449, 467 (2017).
Evidence that the City targeted Grand for
unprecedented administrative burdens, coupled with
the threat of criminal prosecution, unmistakably
establishes that the City “objectively chill[ed]” Grand’s
First Amendment rights. First Choice , 146 S. Ct. at
1127. But the evidence does more than that. The
extraordinary record of religious animus makes this

15
case one of the most glaring violations of the
Constitution’s non-persecution principle to appear
before this Court. See Lukumi, 508 U.S. at 523.
Vindicating Grand’s claims to exercise his religion and
assemble peaceably against ho stile local officials is a
fundamental duty of federal courts. See 42 U.S.C. §
1983. Yet the Sixth Circuit denied his claims as
unripe—for reasons that do not withstand scrutiny.
III. WILLIAMSON COUNTY IS THE WRONG RIPENESS
STANDARD FOR FIRST AMENDMENT CLAIMS—
AND THIS COURT SHOULD SAY SO.
A. The Ripeness Standard Applied Here
Must Fit Grand’s Constitutional Claims.
The widespread practice of religious exercise at
home with fellow believers and the official animus
toward Grand establish the compelling constitutional
stakes. But as the case comes to this Court, “[r]ipeness
is all.” William Shakespeare, King Lear, act 5, sc. 2, l.
12.
The question presented asks whether Williamson
County’s “land-use finality requirement” applies to
Grand’s First Amendment claims. Pet.i. The Sixth
Circuit invoked Williamson County’s ripeness
standard because, in the court’s view, Grand’s First
Amendment claims arise in “the land-use context.” Pet.
App.  7a. Not so. Requiring First Amendment claims to
satisfy a ripeness standard borrowed from the Fifth
Amendment is a category mistake that should be
corrected—not only for Grand’s sake, but for all who
raise claims under the First Amendment.
Ripeness doctrine arises from Article III’s delegation
of “[t]he judicial Power of the United States” to decide
“Cases” and “Controversies.” U.S. Const. art. III, §§ 1,
2. Suggestions that ripeness doctrine also derives from

16
prudential factors untethered from constitutional text
are hard to square with federal courts’ “virtually
unflagging obligation * * * to exercise the jurisdiction
given them.” Colo. River Water Conservation Dist. v.
United States, 424 U.S. 800, 817 (1976); accord Susan
B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, 573 U.S. 149, 167–68
(2014) (same).7
The “basic rationale” of ripeness doctrine “is to
prevent the courts, through avoidance of premature
adjudication, from entangling themselves in abstract
disagreements over administrative policies, and also
to protect the agencies from judicial interference until
an administrative decision has been formalized and its
effects felt in a concrete way by the challenging
parties.” Abbott Lab. v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136, 148–49
(1967), abrogated on other grounds , Califano v.
Sanders, 430 U.S. 99, 105 (1977). Ripeness is ordinarily
measured by “(1) the fitness of the issues for judicial
decision and (2) the hards hip to the parties of
withholding court consideration.” Id. at  149. That
framework prevails today unless a more specific
standard applies. See MedImmune, Inc. v. Genentech,
Inc., 549 U.S. 118, 128 n.8 (2007) (citing Abbott Lab. ).
“Fitness” and “hardship” must be judged by the nature
of the substantive claim. Abbott Lab., 387 U.S. at 149.
That understanding animated Thomas v. Union
Carbide Agric. Prods. Co. , 473 U.S. 568 (1985).
There, pesticide manufacturers challenged a statute
requiring arbitration as a violation of Article III, while
the EPA contended that the claim was unripe because

7 Earlier decisions described ripeness as a function of both
Article III and prudential considerations. See Reno v. Cath. Soc.
Servs., 509 U.S. 43, 57 n.18 (1993). But recent decisions question
the vitality of prudential ripeness or omit it. See Driehaus , 573
U.S. at 167; Trump v. New York, 592 U.S. 125, 131 (2020).

17
the companies had not yet been subjected to
arbitration. Id. at 576, 579. This Court rejected that
argument. The manufacturers’ claim did not turn on
“whether the tribunal awards reasonable compensation but [rather] the tribunal’s authority to adjudicate
the dispute.” Id. at 580.  And the Court held the Article
III challenge ripe, given the “uncertainty and expense
of depending for compensation on a process whose
authority is undermined because its constitutionality
is in question.” Id. at 581.
Thomas teaches that ripeness depends on the
nature of the asserted constitutional right. The Sixth
Circuit neglected that lesson when characterizing this
case as “a land use dispute.” Pet. App.  7a. Grand’s
complaint says otherwise. Count I alleges that the City
and other respondents “have deprived and continue to
deprive [Grand] of his right to free exercise of religion,
as secured by the First Amendment to the United
States Constitution.” Reply App. 83. Count II alleges
that respondents “have deprived and continue[] to
deprive [Grand] of his right to freedom of assembly, as
secured by the First Amendment.” Id. at 84. These are
the claims mentioned in th e question presented. See
Pet.i (referencing “chilled r eligious exercise, worship,
and assembly”).
Because Grand framed his case under the First
Amendment, Williamson County’s finality requirement is a misfit. It holds that “a claim that the
application of government regulations effects a taking
of a property interest is not ripe until the government
entity charged with implementing the regulations has
reached a final decision regarding the application of
the regulations to the property at issue.” 473 U.S. at
186 (emphasis added). This finality test reflects the
perceived requirements of the Fifth Amendment,

18
namely that the “economic impact of [a] challenged
action * * * cannot be evaluated until the administrative agency has arrived at a final, definitive position
regarding how it will apply the regulations * * * to the
particular land in question.” Id. at 191; see id.  at 190
(“Our reluctance to examine taking claims until
such a final decision has been made is compelled by
the very nature of the inquiry required by the Just
Compensation Clause.”). To be sure, the finality
requirement has been relaxed. See Pakdel v. City &
Cnty. of San Francisco, 594 U.S. 474, 478, 480 (2021)
(per curiam) (holding that finality requires evidence
that the government has reached “a conclusive
position”). No matter. The complaint does not seek to
enlarge the permitted uses for Grand’s home. It seeks
redress for constitutional wrongs perpetrated by the
City in prohibiting his religious practice. Reply App.
83. This is a First Amendment case—not a land use
dispute. It follows that the ripeness standard for First
Amendment claims governs.
B. Grand Satisfies the Correct Ripeness
Standard for First Amendment Claims.
1. Settled case law confirms that a claimant alleging
the violation of First Amendment rights may bring a
pre-enforcement challenge under certain conditions.
The leading decision is Driehaus, 573 U.S. at 149.
There, advocacy organizations challenged an Ohio
statute criminalizing false st atements about political
candidates during an election. The Court held that
“the threatened enforcement of law” can satisfy Article
III’s case-or-controversy requirement even without “an
actual arrest, prosecution, or other enforcement
action.” Id. at 158. A claim is justiciable, the Court
explained, when a plaintiff “alleges ‘an intention to
engage in a course of conduct arguably affected with a

19
constitutional interest, but proscribed by a statute,
and there exists a credible threat of prosecution
thereunder.’” Id. at 159 (quoting Babbitt v. United
Farm Workers Nat’l Union, 442 U.S. 289, 298 (1979)).
Although Driehaus was couched in terms of standing,
the Court agreed that “[t]he doctrines of standing and
ripeness ‘originate’ from the same Article III limitation” and “‘boil down to the same question.’” Id. at 158
n.5 (quoting DaimlerChrysler Corp. v. Cuno, 547 U.S.
332, 335 (2006), and MedImmune, 549 U.S. at 128 n.8).
Other decisions likewise affirm that pre-enforcement challenges under the First Amendment can be
ripe for adjudication. See, e.g., Babbitt, 442 U.S. at 298;
Steffel v. Thompson, 415 U.S. 452, 459 (1974).
2. This Court has repeatedly applied Driehaus to
First Amendment claims.
Take a case decided last Term, First Choice, 146 S.
Ct. 1114. There, the New Jersey Attorney General
issued a subpoena demanding that a religious pro-life
pregnancy center produce donor information. The
center sued in federal court under 42 U.S.C. § 1983,
asserting its First Amendment rights. Soon after, the
Attorney General filed his own suit in state court,
“accus[ing] First Choice of violating state law by
failing to comply with his subpoena.” Id. at 1120. The
federal district court dismissed the complaint as nonjusticiable, reasoning that First Choice had not yet
been compelled in the state litigation to disclose
constitutionally protected materials. The Third Circuit
affirmed.
This Court reversed. “[A] litigant may bring a preenforcement suit seeking prospective relief against
government officials so lon g as it faces ‘a credible
threat of enforcement.’” Id.  at 1122 (citing Driehaus,

20
573 U.S. at 161, 164–67). First Choice satisfied that
standard because the Attorney General’s subpoena
“caused it to suffer an actual and ongoing injury to its
First Amendment rights by deterring donors from
associating with it.” Ibid. As the Court confirmed, a
cognizable injury “can also arise when a defendant
burdens a plaintiff’s constitutional rights.” Id. at 1125.
Other decisions have adjudicated pre-enforcement
challenges under the same standard. See, e.g.,
Mahmoud, 606 U.S. at 559–60 (invoking Driehaus in
the context of a free exercise challenge to a controversial reading program for young children); Roman Cath.
Diocese of Brooklyn v.  Cuomo, 592 U.S. 14, 19–20
(2020) (per curiam) (grantin g pre-enforcement relief
from an executive order re stricting attendance at
religious services).
None of these decisions involved a believer who was
fined or arrested or jailed. But all faced the threat of
government sanctions that deterred the exercise of
First Amendment rights—and this Court found those
claims justiciable.
No wonder. First Amendment freedoms are “delicate
and vulnerable, as well as supremely precious in our
society. The threat of sanctions may deter their
exercise almost as potently as the actual application of
sanctions.” NAACP v. Button, 371 U.S. 415, 433 (1963).
Judicial review is indispensable because “[t]he loss of
First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods
of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.”
Elrod v. Burns , 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976). Ripeness
doctrine allows pre-enforcement claims to be promptly
heard to avoid such irreparable injury.
3. Grand’s First Amendment claims are ripe under
Driehaus. That decision requires a claimant to

21
“allege[] ‘an intention to engage in a course of conduct
arguably affected with a constitutional interest, but
proscribed by a statute,” and that there “exist[] a
credible threat of prosecution thereunder.’” Driehaus,
573 U.S. at 159. Each element has support in the
record, which must be construed in the light most
favorable to Grand. See Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.,
477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986) (“The evidence of the nonmovant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences
are to be drawn in his favor.”).
First, Grand plainly expressed his “intention” to
engage in constitutionally protected conduct.
Driehaus, 573 U.S. at 159. He emailed “15 friends to
pray at his home on the upcoming Shabbos.” Reply
App. 9. Grand’s intention is further demonstrated by
his plea for “[p]reliminary and permanent orders
permitting [Grand] to pray with a minyan on Shabbos
and Jewish holidays in his home without obtaining a
[Special Use Permit] from the City.” Id. at 94. Prayer
is a quintessential religious practice secured by the
Free Exercise Clause. See Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch.
Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 512–14 (2022).
Second, Grand’s religious practice is allegedly
“proscribed” by City ordinances. Driehaus, 573 U.S. at
159. The City’s cease-and-desist order says so, Pet.
App.  116a, as did Mayor Brennan, who warned Grand:
“You are under no circumstances allowed to have any
type of religious gathering in your home without first
obtaining a special use permit under Chapter 1274 of
the University Heights Code.” Reply App. 10–11.
Failure to obey that edict, the mayor repeated, “will be
in violation of * * * Chapter 1274 for operating an
illegal synagogue.” Id. at 11.
Third, Grand unquestionably faced “a credible
threat of prosecution” for practicing his religion at

22
home. Driehaus, 573 U.S. at 159.8 Mayor Brennan told
Grand that inviting people to his home to pray “will be
in violation of the cease-and-desist order and the City
will take all legal means available to it.” Reply App. 11.
The Complaint explains that Grand “understood this
as a threat of criminal prosecution if he were to invite
ten friends over to his house to pray.” Ibid.
The cease-and-desist letter issued by the City Law
Director delivered the same threat. The letter accuses
Grand of “intend[ing] to us e [his home] as a place of
religious Assembly” and threatens him with building
code violations if he worshi ps with others without a
Special Use Permit. Pet. App. 116a. The letter says
that “[v]iolation of the City’s ordinances in this
manner may result in building code violations against
you and in the pursuit of additional remedies.” Ibid.
City ordinances make code violations “a misdemeanor
of the first degree,” punishable with imprisonment for
up to six months and a fine  of up to $1,000. Codified
Ordinances of the City of University Heights, Building
and Housing Code § 1420.99(a), (b).
What’s more, Grand was singled out for administrative action. That, “like arrest or prosecution, may give
rise to harm sufficient to justify pre-enforcement
review.” Driehaus, 573 U.S. at 165. A City property
inspector, invoking section 1242.99 of the Planning
and Zoning Code, issued Grand a citation alleging that
a parking area near his ga rage violated City zoning

8 Evidence that Grand confronted “a credible threat of
prosecution” under Driehaus, 573 U.S. at 159, confirms that his
pre-enforcement challenge is ripe. This same evidence likewise
bolsters Grand’s central merits claim—that the City’s response to
his attempt to gather with fellow believers to pray in his home
“objectively chill[ed]” his First Amendment rights. First Choice ,
146 S. Ct. at 1127.

23
ordinances. Reply App. 49, 51. This, although the Code
nowhere forbids using gravel for a residential parking
area. Id. at 52. The citation directed Grand to submit
an appeal “within 15 days of the date of such notice”—
but did not say how or where to present an appeal. Id.
at 50. After getting no response from the City for two
weeks, Grand submitted an appeal to the Board of
Zoning Appeals the same day that he learned that that
was the correct procedure. Id. at 52. The City denied
his appeal. Id. at 52–53. This trumped-up administrative process burdened Grand’s First Amendment
rights. And worse, the citat ion carried the threat of
criminal punishment. See Codified Ordinances of the
City of University Heights, Planning and Zoning
Code § 1242.99 (punishing a violation as a first-
degree misdemeanor with a fine up to $1,000 and/or
imprisonment up to six months).
4. To all this, the City blithely counters that “Grand
could not establish finality and certainly no distinct
harm.” Br. Opp. 13. By its reckoning, “there was no
enforcement action against him, he used the house in
the manner he wished, and Grand remains free to file
a new action if the City applied the ordinance to him
in a way that violates his statutory or constitutional
rights.” Id. at i.
This rigid focus on compliance with local procedure
misapprehends the Bill of Rights—a bulwark against
“[the] threat of sanctions”  specifically because such a
threat “may deter the[] exerci se” of rights “almost as
potently as the actual application of sanctions.”
Button, 371 U.S. at 433. Grand’s complaint amply
satisfies Driehaus. His claims are ripe.

24
C. Williamson County  Cannot Apply to
First Amendment Rights Without Condemning Them to Second-Class Status.
Even so, the Sixth Circuit dismissed Grand’s First
Amendment claims as unripe, reasoning that “Grand
does not point to a final decision implementing the
challenged ordinance.” Pet. App. 8a. The court added
that requiring a final decision “does not unfairly harm
Grand” since he “remains free to file a new action if the
City applies the ordinance to him in a way that
violates his statutory or constitutional rights.” Id. at
11a–12a. Nor did the City’s cease-and-desist letter
matter when, in the court’s view, “[t]he letter is not an
enforcement action, and the City may not enforce it.”
Id. at 13a. And because Grand has “chosen not to
obtain a final decision” regarding a Special Use
Permit, “he is the author of any chilling effect on his
First Amendment interests.” Id. at 13a–14a.
But Williamson County does not control the ripeness
of Grand’s First Amendment claims—Driehaus does. It
is therefore untrue—and cruel—to blame Grand for
the City’s chill on his freedom of religion and assembly .
The decision below falls into a troubling line of lower
court decisions that apply Williamson County to First
Amendment claims with any nexus to land use law.
A leading case is Murphy v. New Milford Zoning
Comm’n, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005). There, a
Christian couple conducted “Sunday afternoon prayer
group meetings” attended by “as many as sixty
participants.” Id. at 345. Neighbors complained about
noise and traffic. Ibid. When the town zoning
commission told the Murphys that the meetings
violated zoning laws—and issued a cease-and-desist
order—they brought a lawsuit asserting “First
Amendment rights to assemble peaceably and to

25
exercise their religion freely” along with statutory
claims. Id. at 345–46.
The Second Circuit characterized the case as a
“zoning dispute” and held that the Murphys’ claims
were ripe only if they produced “a final, definitive
position from a local authority to assess precisely how
they can use their property.” Id. at 347. Acknowledging
that Williamson County originated “in the context of a
regulatory takings challenge,” id. at 349, the court still
applied its finality requirement to the Murphys’ First
Amendment claims. In the court’s view, they had not
“experienced an immediate injury as a result of New
Milford’s actions,” and the court directed the Murphys
“to pursue additional administrative remedies [that]
would further define their alleged injuries.” Id. at 351
(citing Dougherty v. Town of N. Hempstead Bd. of
Zoning Appeals, 282 F.3d 83, 90 (2d Cir. 2002)).
The Third Circuit has similarly distorted ripeness
doctrine by misapplying Williamson County to First
Amendment claims. See, e.g., Felmeister v. Off. of Att’y
Ethics, 856 F.2d 529, 536–37 (3d Cir. 1988) (citing
Williamson County when dismissing as unripe an
attorney’s free speech challenge to New Jersey
restrictions on attorney advertising for lack of finality).
Misapplying Williamson County condemns First
Amendment claims to second-class status merely
because of some touchpoint with land use law. Where
Mahmoud and Cuomo endorse pre-enforcement review
to protect First Amendment rights, see Mahmoud, 606
U.S. at 559–60; Cuomo, 592 U.S. at 19–20, the decision
below and Murphy deny it. See Pet. App.  8a; Murphy,
402 F.3d at 351. Access to judicial relief thus depends
on the accident of whether a local government chooses
to suppress First Amendment rights through land
use law or through some other means. Second-class

26
treatment inflicts real-world costs. Losing the right to
exercise one’s religion or to assemble with others freely
is not merely harmful—but irreparably so. See Elrod,
427 U.S. at 373.
This case demonstrates why Williamson County
must be confined to Fifth Amendment claims. Allowing
its casual doctrinal drift has transformed claims like
Grand’s into rights without a remedy. See Marbury v.
Madison, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137, 163 (1803) (affirming
“the right of every individual to claim the protection of
the laws, whenever he receives an injury”). Ripeness
doctrine exists to confine federal judicial power to
cases and controversies, not to thwart valid claims.
Grand is not the first litigant whose First Amendment
claims have foundered on the shoals of Williamson
County—but let him be the last.
CONCLUSION
Early in his administration, President Washington
reassured a Jewish congregation that the United
States government “gives to bigotry no sanction, to
persecution no assistance.” Letter from George
Washington to the Hebrew Congregation in Newport,
R.I. (Aug. 18, 1790), reprinted in George Washington,
Writings 767 (John Rhodehamel ed., 1997). And he
closed his letter with a blessing: “May the Children of
the Stock of Abraham, who dwell in this land, continue
to merit and enjoy the good will of the other
inhabitants; while every one shall sit in safety under
his own vine and figtree, and there shall be none to
make him afraid.” Ibid.
The City of University Heights strayed from
Washington’s generous conception of religious freedom
by demanding a permit and threatening criminal
prosecution merely because Grand sought to worship

27
with fellow believers in his own home. His claims are
rooted in the Constitution’s shelter for religious
exercise in the home as a personal refuge—where
“there shall be none to make him afraid.” Ibid. The
Sixth Circuit was wrong to deem his claims unripe. Its
judgment should be reversed.
